summary: Describes ISO-2022-JP-2, a multilingual extension of the Japanese ISO-2022-JP text encoding, used experimentally in mail and network news in several Japanese networks.

eli5.summary: Japanese text uses a special way of switching between alphabets inside a message. This memo stretches that scheme to cover more languages.

questions: how does iso-2022 escape sequence switching work
which character sets does iso-2022-jp-2 support
subtitle: A 7-bit text encoding that lets one email or news message mix Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Greek and Latin-1 text.

tldr.problem: ISO-2022-JP covers English and Japanese, but messages sometimes need other scripts such as Korean, Chinese, Greek or accented Latin letters.
tldr.mechanism: ISO-2022-JP-2 starts in ASCII and uses ISO 2022 escape sequences to switch among a fixed set of 94-character and 96-character sets, all within 7 bits.
tldr.outcome: It is named for use in the MIME charset parameter and was in experimental use for mail and news in several Japanese networks.

today: RFC 1554 is an Informational memo from December 1993 and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes an encoding used experimentally in several Japanese networks at the time of writing.

sections.title: A Multilingual Extension
sections.content:
RFC 1554 describes ISO-2022-JP-2, a text encoding used experimentally for electronic mail and network news messages in several Japanese networks. It extends ISO-2022-JP, the existing Japanese encoding, and is supported by an Emacs-based multilingual editor called MULE.

The name is meant for the charset parameter of MIME headers.
sections.eli5: It is an upgrade of the Japanese text code so one message can also hold other languages.

sections.title: How the Encoding Works
sections.content:
Text starts in ASCII and switches to other ISO 2022 character sets using a limited set of escape sequences. All characters are encoded with 7 bits. 94-character sets are designated to G0 and invoked as GL. 96-character sets are designated to G2 and used one character at a time with the single shift ESC N.

For example, ESC $ ( C announces that the following bytes are Korean KSC characters, two bytes each. ESC . A designates ISO 8859-1 to G2, and then ESC N A stands for the character A with acute.

Escape sequences announce which set follows, much like switching a keyboard layout; a decoder reads them to know how to interpret each byte.
sections.eli5: A secret marker says 'the next letters are Korean', and another marker switches back to plain English letters.

sections.title: The Character Sets and Escape Sequences
sections.content:
The RFC lists seven 94-character sets designated to G0: ASCII, JIS X 0208-1978, JIS X 0208-1983, JIS X 0201-Roman, GB2312-1980, KSC5601-1987 and JIS X 0212-1990. It also lists two 96-character sets designated to G2: ISO 8859-1 and ISO 8859-7 (Greek).

Use of JIS X 0201-Roman is allowed for backward compatibility with ISO-2022-JP but is discouraged.
sections.eli5: There is a short menu of alphabets you can switch to, and each has its own marker.

sections.title: Line and Text Rules
sections.content:
If any G0 designation appears in the text, there must be a switch to ASCII or JIS X 0201-Roman before a space character or control characters such as tab or CRLF. So the next line starts in the character set switched to before the previous line ended. Programs that seek randomly in a file, such as pagers and editors, may assume lines begin with ASCII.

At the start of each line, the G2 designation of the previous line is cleared, so a new one must be given before any 96-character-set character is used. The text must end in ASCII designated to G0. Left-to-right direction is assumed for horizontal display.

The RFC also gives a formal syntax in the notation of RFC 822. It warns that some transports, such as old Bnews, cannot relay the 7-bit value 7/15 (decimal 127), which encodes, for example, y with diaeresis of ISO 8859-1.
sections.eli5: Every line must start and end back in plain letters, so a reader can jump to any line and still make sense of it.

sections.title: Use with MIME
sections.content: In a MIME message the encoding is declared as Content-Type: text/plain; charset=iso-2022-jp-2. Because the encoding is already 7-bit, no Content-Transfer-Encoding header is needed, and applying Base64 or Quoted-Printable would make the message unreadable in software that is not MIME-compliant. The encoding may also be used in MIME headers, where both B and Q encoding could be useful.
sections.eli5: The label on the envelope says which code the letter uses, and the letter needs no extra wrapping.
